nodes.label: Mutalibov
nodes.full: Ayaz Mutalibov, the last Communist leader of the republic, became president in 1990, was confirmed in an uncontested vote on 8 September 1991 and presided over the declaration of independence; after the killing at Khojaly in February 1992 he resigned on 6 March under pressure; after the fall of Shusha on 8 May the old parliament briefly restored him, and he was ousted again on 15 May by the Popular Front, and he lived in Russia until his death.
nodes.src: Tadeusz Swietochowski, Russia and Azerbaijan (1995); Audrey Altstadt, The Politics of Culture in Soviet Azerbaijan (2016); de Waal, Black Garden (2003).

nodes.label: Elchibey
nodes.full: Abulfaz Elchibey, a historian and former dissident who led the Popular Front, was elected president on 7 June 1992 with about 59 per cent in Azerbaijan's first genuinely competitive presidential election; his government took the country out of the CIS, looked to Turkey and the West and lost the district of Kelbajar to Armenian forces, and after the rebellion of Colonel Surat Huseynov in Gyanja he left Baku on 18 June 1993 for his home in Nakhchivan. He died in Ankara in 2000.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (1992); Swietochowski 1995; de Waal 2003.

nodes.label: Heydar Aliyev
nodes.full: Heydar Aliyev, the former Soviet Politburo member and Communist chief of Azerbaijan, who had been in Nakhchivan since 1990, was called to Baku in June 1993 as parliament speaker and was elected president in October 1993 and again in 1998. He ended the army's rebellions, signed the ceasefire of May 1994, concluded the Contract of the Century with Western oil companies in 1994 and built a centralised presidential system and a party of power; his supporters stress the stability and the oil strategy, his critics the repression and the dynastic transfer. He died in the United States on 12 December 2003.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (1993, 1998); Swietochowski 1995; OSCE/ODIHR reports; Svante Cornell, Azerbaijan since Independence (2011).

nodes.label: Ilham Aliyev
nodes.full: Ilham Aliyev, Heydar's son and a former vice-president of the state oil company, was named prime minister in August 2003 and elected president in October 2003, and re-elected in 2008, 2013, 2018 and, in an early election on 7 February 2024, with about 92 per cent. The referendum of 2009 removed the limit on terms and the one of 2016 extended the term to seven years and created the posts of vice-presidents; the OSCE/ODIHR has repeatedly judged the elections as lacking genuine competition. As of 2026 he is head of state.
nodes.src: Central Electoral Commission records (2003–2024); OSCE/ODIHR election reports; Constitution of Azerbaijan, referendum results (2009, 2016).

nodes.label: Mehriban Aliyeva
nodes.full: Mehriban Aliyeva, the president's wife, a member of the parliament since 2005 and head of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, was named first vice-president by decree on 21 February 2017 under the constitutional change of 2016, with the office placing her first in the line of succession; the government describes the appointment as an expression of the foundation's work and of the trust of the president, and the opposition and some outside analysts as a step in the dynastic nature of the system.
nodes.src: Presidential decree (21 February 2017); Constitution of Azerbaijan, as amended (2016); press reports.

nodes.label: Governments of the first years
nodes.full: The prime ministers of the first years were Panah Huseynov (1992–1993), Surat Huseynov (1993–1994), the Gyanja colonel whose rebellion had brought down Elchibey and who was himself dismissed after he challenged Aliyev in October 1994, and Fuad Guliyev (1994–1996); the cabinets were weak against the army and the militias.
nodes.src: Government records; Swietochowski 1995; Cornell 2011.

nodes.label: Rasizade
nodes.full: Artur Rasizade, a Soviet-era economist and an ethnic Azerbaijani born in Gyanja who had been the Soviet-period premier of Azerbaijan, was prime minister for twenty-one years from November 1996 to April 2018 under both presidents, and presided over the oil-boom budgets and the devaluation crises of 2015.
nodes.src: Presidential decrees (1996, 2018); Cornell 2011.

nodes.label: Mammadov and Asadov
nodes.full: Novruz Mammadov, a long-time presidential assistant, was prime minister from April 2018 to October 2019, and Ali Asadov, a long-serving official of the presidential administration, has held the office since 8 October 2019; the governments have run the reconstruction of the districts recovered in 2020 and 2023 and the programme of return.
nodes.src: Presidential decrees (2018, 2019); government statements.

nodes.label: Khojaly
nodes.full: On the night of 25–26 February 1992 Armenian forces, with elements of the former Soviet 366th regiment, took the town of Khojaly near Stepanakert, and many of the civilians who fled were killed in the surrounding fields and forests; the Azerbaijani government counts 613 killed, Memorial's investigation found about 485, and Human Rights Watch concluded that at least 200 civilians had been killed. Azerbaijan, which commemorates it on 26 February and calls it a genocide, treats it as the main crime of the war; Armenian sources dispute the figures and the intent and argue that a corridor had been offered, and some accounts, among them Armenian ones, point also to the political struggle in Baku.
nodes.src: Human Rights Watch, Bloodshed in the Caucasus (1992); Memorial reports (1992); de Waal 2003; Azerbaijani parliament's declaration (1994).

nodes.label: First Karabakh war
nodes.full: In 1992–1994, after the withdrawal of Soviet forces and the collapse of the army, Azerbaijani forces lost Shusha in May 1992, Kelbajar in April 1993, Agdam in July 1993 and the southern districts of Fuzuli, Jebrail, Gubadli and Zangilan in the autumn; the Azerbaijani account describes this as an aggression and occupation of some 20 per cent of the state's territory, with about 600,000 or more internally displaced persons, some 20,000–30,000 killed in all, and the UN Security Council resolutions of 1993 demanding withdrawal. The ceasefire of 12 May 1994 held, with violations, until 2016.
nodes.src: UN Security Council resolutions 822, 853, 874, 884 (1993); Human Rights Watch, Azerbaijan: Seven Years of Conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh (1994); de Waal 2003.

nodes.label: Rebellions of 1993–1995
nodes.full: In June 1993 the colonel Surat Huseynov marched from Gyanja on Baku and Elchibey fled; in October 1994 a plot by Huseynov, then prime minister, and the deputy interior minister Rovshan Javadov was put down by Aliyev with popular support, and in March 1995 the special police unit OMON rebelled and was suppressed with losses. The episodes established the president's control of the security forces.
nodes.src: Swietochowski 1995; Cornell 2011; de Waal 2003.

nodes.label: Baku metro bombings
nodes.full: Two bombs in the Baku metro on 19 March and 3 July 1994 killed some 27 people and injured many more; the authorities attributed them to Armenian intelligence working with Lezgin separatists (the Sadval group), some of whom were convicted, and the full responsibility has not been established independently.
nodes.src: Azerbaijani court records (1995–1996); Cornell 2011.

nodes.label: Nardaran
nodes.full: In the Shia village of Nardaran near Baku, special forces raided the home of the leader of the Muslim Unity Movement, Taleh Bagirzade, on 26 November 2015 and several people were killed, among them two police officers; the government said that it was an armed group planning a coup and an Iranian-supported plot, and Bagirzade and others were sentenced to long prison terms, while rights groups said that the movement was a religious one and the trial unfair.
nodes.src: Court and Prosecutor-General's statements (2015–2016); Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International reports.

nodes.label: April war of 2016
nodes.full: In the heaviest fighting since 1994 Azerbaijani forces regained the heights of Lalatapa in Jebrail and positions near Talish within four days, in a battle that Baku presented as a response to Armenian shelling; Azerbaijan reported 31 soldiers killed and Armenia 92, with civilian victims on both sides, and a ceasefire was mediated by Russia.
nodes.src: Ministries of defence of Azerbaijan and Armenia (April 2016); OSCE Minsk Group statements.

nodes.label: 44-day war
nodes.full: After clashes on the Tovuz border in July 2020, in which a general, Polad Hashimov, was killed, the war started on 27 September; Azerbaijan, with Turkish and Israeli drones and Turkish support, recovered the districts of Fuzuli, Jebrail, Zangilan and Gubadli, Hadrut and, on 8 November, Shusha, and the trilateral statement of 9–10 November restored Agdam, Kelbajar and Lachin to its control and brought in Russian peacekeepers. The Azerbaijani state calls it the Patriotic War and the Victory, commemorated on 8 November; its military dead were officially announced as about 2,800–2,900, with civilians killed by missiles at Gyanja and Barda, and the Armenian side describes it as an aggression and attributes the civilian victims to Azerbaijan's attacks on towns, while the two sides have accused each other of war crimes.
nodes.src: Trilateral statement (10 November 2020); Azerbaijani Ministry of Defence; Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International reports (2020–2021).

nodes.label: Gyanja and Barda
nodes.full: Missile and rocket strikes on Gyanja on 4, 11 and 17 October and on Barda on 27–28 October 2020 killed several dozen civilians, 21 in Barda and 14 in the strike of 17 October at Gyanja; Azerbaijan holds Armenian forces responsible, Amnesty International concluded that Barda was hit with cluster munitions from Armenian-controlled territory, and Armenian officials deny that they targeted civilian areas and said the strikes were aimed at military objects.
nodes.src: Amnesty International, Armenia/Azerbaijan: Use of Cluster Munitions (2020); Human Rights Watch (2020); statements of the two governments.

nodes.label: Operation of September 2023
nodes.full: On 19 September 2023 Azerbaijan launched what it called local anti-terror measures against the military installations of the Karabakh Armenians, and within a day the authorities of Stepanakert agreed to disarm and to talks in Yevlakh; in Baku's account about 190 of its soldiers were killed, and the Armenians of Karabakh left in the following days. The Azerbaijani government says that it offered them integration as citizens and denies expulsion, while Armenia, the Karabakh authorities and many observers speak of ethnic cleansing; on 15 October 2023 Aliyev raised the flag in Khankendi, the former Stepanakert.
nodes.src: Azerbaijani Ministry of Defence statements (September 2023); UN visiting mission report (October 2023); Armenian government statements.

nodes.label: Restoration of independence
nodes.full: After the failed coup in Moscow the Supreme Soviet declared the restoration of independence on 30 August 1991, in succession to the republic of 1918–1920, and passed the Constitutional Act on the State Independence of the Republic of Azerbaijan on 18 October 1991; a referendum of 29 December 1991, which the Karabakh Armenians did not take part in, confirmed it, and on 26 November the parliament had abolished the Nagorno-Karabakh autonomous oblast.
nodes.src: Declaration of 30 August 1991; Constitutional Act of 18 October 1991; Swietochowski 1995.

nodes.label: Constitution and referendums
nodes.full: The constitution adopted by referendum on 12 November 1995 established a strong presidency, which the referendum of 2002 changed the line of succession, the referendum of 18 March 2009 abolished the two-term limit, and that of 26 September 2016 extended the term to seven years, created the vice-presidents and gave the president the right to dissolve parliament; the Venice Commission criticised the last as concentrating power.
nodes.src: Constitution of Azerbaijan (1995, as amended); Venice Commission opinion (2016).

nodes.label: Elections and observers
nodes.full: International observers from the OSCE and the Council of Europe judged the elections of the Aliyev era, from 1998, to fall short of the standards, with a lack of real competition, restrictions on assembly and a dominance of the ruling party in the media; the presidential election of 2013 was criticised by the OSCE and praised by some other observers, and for the early election of February 2024 the OSCE/ODIHR did not deploy because Baku limited the number of observers it would admit. The opposition and Western governments call the results manufactured, and the government says that they reflect the voters' choice.
nodes.src: OSCE/ODIHR election observation reports (1998–2024); PACE reports.

nodes.label: Alphabet reform
nodes.full: The Latin alphabet was adopted in 1991 and the reform was confirmed by Heydar Aliyev's decree on the alphabet and language reform that took effect on 1 August 2001, after the Soviet decades of the Cyrillic script, and the state language was defined as Azerbaijani rather than Turkish; the transition and the cutting of the written tradition from the Cyrillic and Arabic scripts are considered among the main cultural changes of the period.
nodes.src: Law of 1991; Presidential decree (18 June 2001); Altstadt 2016.

nodes.label: NGO laws and arrests
nodes.full: Amendments of 2013–2014 to the laws on NGOs and grants required the registration of foreign funding and the government's approval, and in 2014 the human rights defenders Leyla Yunus, Rasul Jafarov and Arif Yunus, the investigative journalist Khadija Ismayilova and others were arrested and given prison terms on charges of tax evasion, illegal business and treason; the European Court of Human Rights found violations in several cases, and the government describes the cases as ordinary criminal matters.
nodes.src: Laws of Azerbaijan (2013–2014); European Court of Human Rights judgments (Ilgar Mammadov v. Azerbaijan, 2014; Rasul Jafarov v. Azerbaijan, 2016); Human Rights Watch reports.

nodes.label: Media law and Abzas Media
nodes.full: The media law of 2022 introduced a register of journalists and restricted the media's financing, and from November 2023 the police arrested the staff of the investigative outlet Abzas Media and later of Meydan TV and Toplum TV on charges of smuggling currency, money-laundering and tax evasion; on 20 June 2025 a Baku court sentenced the Abzas Media director Ulvi Hasanli and others to between seven and a half and nine years, and the appeals were rejected in September 2025. The Committee to Protect Journalists counts at least twenty-one journalists jailed since late 2023, and the government says that the defendants are tried for financial crimes.
nodes.src: Law on Media (2021); Baku Grave Crimes Court verdict (20 June 2025); CPJ and RSF reports (2025).

nodes.label: Treaty and Armenian constitution
nodes.full: Azerbaijan holds that the treaty on peace and interstate relations initialled in Washington on 8 August 2025 will be signed only when Armenia amends the constitution, whose preamble refers to the Declaration of Independence of 1990 and its mention of the unification with Karabakh, which Baku regards as a territorial claim; President Aliyev said at the Munich Security Conference in February 2026 that he would sign the day after the change. Armenia has begun the work on a new constitution with a referendum planned for 2027, and as of October 2026 the treaty is not signed.
nodes.src: Joint declaration of Washington (8 August 2025); statements of President Aliyev (2025–2026); Armenian government decisions (2026).

nodes.label: Muslims Office and the state
nodes.full: Azerbaijan is a secular state with a Muslim population of whom roughly two thirds are Shia and the rest Sunni; the Caucasus Muslims Office under Sheikh-ul-Islam Allahshukur Pashazade, in office since 1980, is the official body for both, the State Committee for Work with Religious Associations controls registration and the importation of literature, and the Heydar Mosque and the Juma Mosque in Baku are the principal places of worship. Since 2010 the state has banned the hijab in school classes, and religious groups that are not under the Office's control are regulated.
nodes.src: Law on Freedom of Religious Belief (1992, 2009 amendments); State Committee reports; US State Department religious freedom reports.

nodes.label: Jews, Udis and Orthodox
nodes.full: The state presents itself as a country of multiculturalism and tolerance: the Mountain Jews of Krasnaya Sloboda near Quba, where the synagogue and the village are a centre of the community in Azerbaijan, the Udi Christians of Nij, the Russian Orthodox, and the small Catholic and Lutheran communities have been given attention in official events such as the Baku Process on intercultural dialogue and the year of multiculturalism of 2016.
nodes.src: State Committee for Work with Religious Associations; Baku International Humanitarian Forum (2010–); US State Department reports.

nodes.label: Religious heritage in Karabakh
nodes.full: After 2020 the control of the districts and Shusha, with the Armenian Ghazanchetsots Cathedral, which was struck in October 2020 and later restored with changes to its dome, and the mosques of Aghdam, which were damaged during the occupation, made the heritage a field of contested accounts: Azerbaijan describes the churches as monuments of the Caucasian Albanians, its own ancestors, and the destruction of its mosques in the Armenian-controlled districts as a crime, and Armenian institutions and many outside experts document threats to Armenian churches, khachkars and cemeteries and the removal of Armenian inscriptions; UNESCO has sought access and monitoring.
nodes.src: UNESCO statements (2020–2024); ICJ order of 7 December 2021; Azerbaijani and Armenian Ministries of Culture statements; Caucasus Heritage Watch reports.

nodes.label: Mugham
nodes.full: The classical modal music of mugham, associated with singers such as Alim Qasimov and the tar and kamancha players, was proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2003 and inscribed on the Representative List in 2008, and the International Mugham Centre in Baku, opened in 2008, put it in a purpose-built hall.
nodes.src: UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage; Azerbaijan Ministry of Culture.

nodes.label: Eurovision and Heydar Aliyev Center
nodes.full: The duo Ell and Nikki won the Eurovision Song Contest of 2011 in Düsseldorf with Running Scared, and Baku hosted it in 2012 in the new Crystal Hall, with a national campaign of building; in May 2012 the Heydar Aliyev Center, designed by Zaha Hadid, and the Flame Towers on the city's hill opened as the landmarks of the oil era. The contest also drew attention to human rights restrictions in the country.
nodes.src: European Broadcasting Union records (2011, 2012); Heydar Aliyev Center; Human Rights Watch reports (2012).

nodes.label: Chess and the Baku games
nodes.full: Azerbaijan, the birthplace of Garry Kasparov and of the grandmasters Teimour Radjabov and Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, hosted the first European Games in June 2015, the Formula 1 Grand Prix in the streets of Baku from 2016 and the Chess Olympiad of 2016; the events were presented as state prestige projects, with the criticism that they were accompanied by the repression of critics.
nodes.src: European Olympic Committees; FIDE records; Human Rights Watch reports (2015).

nodes.label: Azerbaijanism and the Turkic idea
nodes.full: The Popular Front under Elchibey promoted an identity based on a common Turkic origin and on language; Heydar Aliyev formulated the doctrine of Azerbaijanism, which defined the nation as a political one of all citizens, with the slogan of one nation, two states used for Turkey; later governments combined these with the cultural nationalism of the Caucasian Albanian past and the language of victory.
nodes.src: Altstadt 2016; Cornell 2011; Swietochowski 1995.

nodes.label: Victory Day and Trophy Park
nodes.full: Azerbaijan celebrates the Victory Day on 8 November, and the Military Trophy Park opened in Baku in April 2021 displays captured Armenian equipment, helmets and, in the original display, wax figures of Armenian soldiers; Armenia and some outside commentators criticised the display as dehumanising, and Baku says that it is a museum of the war.
nodes.src: Presidential decrees (2020, 2021); press reports and statements of the two governments.

nodes.label: Western Azerbaijan
nodes.full: From 2021–2022 President Aliyev and a new community of Western Azerbaijanis, set up in December 2022, have spoken of the right of return of the Azerbaijanis who left Armenia in 1988–1991 and used the name Western Azerbaijan for the territory of Armenia; the government says that it is a humanitarian right to return, and Armenia sees an expression of a territorial claim, a question linked to the demand for a change of the Armenian constitution.
nodes.src: Statements of President Aliyev (2021–2026); Western Azerbaijan Community; Armenian Ministry of Foreign Affairs statements.

nodes.label: Contract of the Century
nodes.full: The production-sharing agreement of 20 September 1994 between the State Oil Company of Azerbaijan and a consortium of eleven companies from the United States, Britain, Russia, Turkey and others for the development of the Azeri–Chirag–Guneshli fields, signed at the Gulistan Palace, brought tens of billions of dollars of investment and made oil the basis of the state; a similar agreement of 1996 and later contracts developed Shah Deniz.
nodes.src: Production sharing agreement (1994); BP and SOCAR documents; Cornell 2011.

nodes.label: Oil fund and the boom
nodes.full: The State Oil Fund (SOFAZ), established in 1999, collected the revenues, and as the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline came on stream the gross domestic product grew by more than 25 per cent a year in 2005–2007, a rate near the world's highest, with a poverty rate that fell from about half of the population in 2001 to some 6 per cent by 2013 according to official figures; the economy remained dependent on oil, and non-oil sectors and the exchange rate were exposed to its price.
nodes.src: State Oil Fund annual reports; World Bank and IMF reports; State Statistical Committee.

nodes.label: Devaluations of 2015
nodes.full: After the oil price fell in 2014, the central bank devalued the manat by about a third in February 2015 and let it float on 21 December, so that it lost nearly half of its value against the dollar; the bank crisis, the rise in prices and the fall in real incomes followed, and the government's responses included restrictions on the banking sector and a programme of non-oil development.
nodes.src: Central Bank of Azerbaijan decisions (2015); IMF Article IV reports.

nodes.label: Azerbaijani Laundromat
nodes.full: In 2017 the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and partner newspapers reported that about 2.9 billion dollars had passed in 2012–2014 through four British shell companies and the Danske Bank branch in Estonia to buy luxury goods and to pay European politicians and others; the Azerbaijani government rejected the allegations as a campaign, and the Council of Europe's investigation found that members of its assembly had been involved.
nodes.src: OCCRP, The Azerbaijani Laundromat (2017); Council of Europe independent investigation body report (2018).

nodes.label: Gas for Europe
nodes.full: The Southern Gas Corridor of the Shah Deniz fields, the South Caucasus Pipeline, the Trans-Anatolian and the Trans-Adriatic pipelines, began deliveries to Italy at the end of 2020; after Russia's invasion of Ukraine the European Commission and Azerbaijan signed a memorandum on 18 July 2022 to double the gas exports to Europe to about 20 billion cubic metres a year by 2027, and Azerbaijan became a significant supplier, though its capacity is a fraction of the Russian volumes that Europe had lost.
nodes.src: EU–Azerbaijan memorandum (18 July 2022); BP and SOCAR reports.

nodes.label: Great Return and reconstruction
nodes.full: The government has budgeted several billion manats a year for the rebuilding of the districts recovered in 2020 and 2023, including the airports of Fuzuli (2021), Zangilan (2022) and Lachin (2024), roads, the Horadiz–Aghband railway, smart villages and the resettlement of the displaced under a Great Return programme to be completed by 2040; as of March 2026 independent counts put the returnees at about 30,000 people in some 40 settlements against official targets of more, and analysts cite mines, jobs and land questions as slowing the pace.
nodes.src: Presidential decrees on the Great Return Programme (2022–2023); Caucasian Knot reports (2026); ANAMA data.

nodes.label: BTC and Southern Gas Corridor
nodes.full: The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline, 1,768 kilometres long and opened on 25 May 2005 at Sangachal, carried the first oil to the Mediterranean terminal at Ceyhan in July 2006, and the Southern Gas Corridor, completed in 2020, extended the route for gas to Italy; the projects reduced the regional dependence on Russian routes and were criticised by environmental groups.
nodes.src: BP and SOCAR documents; Cornell 2011.

nodes.label: Alat port
nodes.full: The new Baku International Sea Trade Port at Alat, which began operations in 2018 with a Free Economic Zone, together with the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway and the Caspian ferry routes, was designed as a hub of the Middle Corridor linking China and Central Asia with Europe avoiding Russia, and its use rose after 2022.
nodes.src: Baku International Sea Trade Port documents; Azerbaijan Railways statements.

nodes.label: Azerspace and airports
nodes.full: The first Azerbaijani telecommunications satellite, Azerspace-1, was launched in February 2013 by an Ariane 5 from Kourou, and Baku is the country's aviation hub; after 2020 the new airports at Fuzuli, Zangilan and Lachin were built in the districts retaken and are cited as part of the programme of reconstruction.
nodes.src: Azercosmos documents; Presidential decrees.

nodes.label: Turkey and the Shusha Declaration
nodes.full: Turkey, which was the first state to recognise independence in 1991, has been Azerbaijan's closest partner, with the slogan of one nation, two states, the closure of the Armenian border in 1993, military training and arms and, in the war of 2020, drones, advisers and political support; the Shusha Declaration on allied relations signed on 15 June 2021 contains a mutual-assistance clause, and the Organization of Turkic States, whose origin is the Nakhchivan agreement of 2009, is a further framework.
nodes.src: Shusha Declaration (15 June 2021); Nakhchivan Agreement (2009); Cornell 2011.

nodes.label: Russia and the CIS
nodes.full: Azerbaijan joined the CIS in September 1993 under Aliyev, leased the Gabala radar station to Russia until it was closed in 2012, signed the Caspian convention in Aktau on 12 August 2018 and maintained a cautious balance with Moscow; relations became tense in 2024–2025 after the crash of an Azerbaijan Airlines flight near Aktau on 25 December 2024, in which 38 of 67 aboard died, which Baku attributed to Russian air defence fire, the raids in Yekaterinburg in June 2025 and the arrests of Sputnik Azerbaijan staff, and Putin publicly apologised in Dushanbe on 9 October 2025 and the two sides agreed on compensation in April 2026, though the relations remain uneven.
nodes.src: Caspian convention (2018); Azerbaijani and Russian official statements (2024–2026); OC Media and Eurasianet reports.

nodes.label: Israel and Iran
nodes.full: Israel, which has been a major buyer of Azerbaijani oil and a supplier of drones and other arms, opened an embassy in Baku in 1993 and Azerbaijan opened one in Tel Aviv in March 2023; relations with Iran, which has a large Azerbaijani minority, have been tense over the Caspian, religion and Baku's ties with Israel, with an armed attack on the Azerbaijani embassy in Tehran on 27 January 2023, though they have shown cooperation in the Aras River dam projects and the Araz corridor.
nodes.src: Azerbaijani and Iranian Ministries of Foreign Affairs statements; press reports.

nodes.label: Section 907
nodes.full: Section 907 of the Freedom Support Act of 1992, passed under the influence of the Armenian-American lobby, banned direct US aid to the Azerbaijani government until it ended the blockades against Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh, and has been waived by presidents since 2002 for security cooperation; the relationship has been marked by cooperation on energy and in Afghanistan and by American criticism of the human rights situation, and after the Washington summit of August 2025 further changes in the restrictions were reported, details of which are not independently verified as of 2026.
nodes.src: Freedom Support Act, Section 907 (1992); presidential waivers (2002–); statements after the Washington meeting (August 2025).

nodes.label: EU and Council of Europe
nodes.full: Azerbaijan joined the Council of Europe in 2001 and signed a memorandum on strategic partnership in energy with the EU in 2006 and in July 2022; in January 2024 the Parliamentary Assembly refused to ratify the powers of its delegation, and Azerbaijan then suspended its participation in the assembly, so that the relationship with the Council is limited as of 2026, while the energy partnership with the EU continues.
nodes.src: PACE decisions (January 2024); EU–Azerbaijan memoranda (2006, 2022).

nodes.label: Non-Aligned chair
nodes.full: Azerbaijan, a member of the Non-Aligned Movement since 2011, held the chair for 2019–2023 after its Baku summit of October 2019, and used the position, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the Organization of Turkic States to present its position on the Karabakh question.
nodes.src: Non-Aligned Movement documents (2019); Azerbaijani Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

nodes.label: The displaced
nodes.full: Some 600,000 or more Azerbaijanis, from Karabakh and the seven surrounding districts and also from Armenia, were displaced by the conflict, one of the largest displaced populations in the world in proportion to its population; for years they lived in camps, railway wagons and unfinished buildings, and from 2001 the government and the oil fund built settlements for them, so that the number in poor housing fell from several hundred thousand in the 1990s.
nodes.src: UNHCR and State Committee for Refugees and IDPs figures; Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre reports.

nodes.label: The mines
nodes.full: The districts recovered after 2020 and 2023 are among the most heavily mined areas in the world, with a contamination estimated by the national mine action agency ANAMA at up to a million mines and unexploded items, and hundreds of people, soldiers and civilians, have been killed or injured since the 2020 ceasefire; the question of the maps of the minefields that Armenia holds has been raised by Azerbaijan in the peace talks.
nodes.src: ANAMA reports; HALO Trust and ICRC statements (2021–2025).

nodes.label: Caspian and COP29
nodes.full: The level of the Caspian Sea has fallen by well over a metre since the mid-1990s, with scientists projecting a further fall under climate change, with effects on the ports, the ecology and the sturgeon; Azerbaijan hosted the UN Climate Change Conference COP29 in Baku in November 2024, which set a new goal of 300 billion dollars a year by 2035 in climate finance for developing countries, while itself a major exporter of oil and gas.
nodes.src: UNFCCC decision on the New Collective Quantified Goal (2024); Caspian Environment Programme reports.

nodes.label: Covid-19
nodes.full: The first case was recorded on 28 February 2020 and a special quarantine regime, with restrictions on movement, lasted with interruptions until 2021; about 10,000 deaths were officially reported by 2022 and the vaccination campaign started in January 2021.
nodes.src: Operational Headquarters under the Cabinet of Ministers; WHO data.

nodes.label: The missing
nodes.full: The state commission on prisoners of war, hostages and missing persons lists nearly four thousand citizens missing from the wars of the 1990s and about a hundred from the war of 2020, and the families have followed the work of search and identification with the ICRC; the discovery of mass graves in the districts has been reported, and Armenia has raised parallel cases of its own.
nodes.src: State Commission of Azerbaijan on Prisoners of War, Hostages and Missing Persons; ICRC reports.

nodes.label: Women and domestic violence law
nodes.full: The law on the prevention of domestic violence of 2010 and the State Committee for Family, Women and Children Affairs, established in 2006, formed the official framework, women hold under a fifth of the seats in the parliament, and in 2017 the president's wife became the first vice-president; human rights groups report that the shelters and the enforcement are limited and that sex-selective abortion has been among the highest in the world.
nodes.src: Law on Prevention of Domestic Violence (2010); UN CEDAW Committee reviews; UNFPA reports.

nodes.label: Talysh, Lezgins and others
nodes.full: The Talysh of the south, the Lezgins of the north, the Avars, the Tats, the Kurds and the Udis make up a few per cent of the population in the census; the Talysh language and the Talysh people's identity were politically suppressed, as shown in the arrest of the scholar Novruzali Mammadov in 2007 who died in prison in 2009, and the questions of education in minority languages and of the Lezgin borderland with Russia are sensitive.
nodes.src: State Statistical Committee census (2009); Human Rights Watch and Council of Europe reports; Minority Rights Group.

nodes.label: Political prisoners
nodes.full: Local and international human rights organisations have counted over a hundred political prisoners in the 2010s and, in the last years, more than three hundred in the lists of local groups, among them journalists, activists, opposition figures and researchers; the European Court of Human Rights has found violations in cases such as Ilgar Mammadov's, and the government rejects the term and holds that those detained were sentenced for crimes.
nodes.src: European Court of Human Rights judgments; Union for Freedom of Political Prisoners lists; Council of Europe and UN reports.

nodes.label: Migrants in Russia
nodes.full: Hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis, in the trade of fruit and vegetables, in construction and in services, live in Russia, in a diaspora counted in some figures at over a million, and their remittances were an important source of household income; the raids against Azerbaijani families in Yekaterinburg in June 2025, in which two brothers died, were a sign of the tensions between the two states and affected the community.
nodes.src: State Statistical Committee; World Bank remittance data; press reports (2025).

nodes.label: The Karabakh movement and Black January
nodes.full: The Karabakh movement of 1988, the Sumgait pogrom, the violence against Armenians of 1988–1990 and the Soviet army’s entry into Baku in January 1990 prepared the independence of the republic and the first war.

nodes.label: The Azerbaijan Democratic Republic
nodes.full: The Azerbaijan Democratic Republic, proclaimed on 28 May 1918 and ended by the Red Army in April 1920, was the first republic in the Muslim world and the model in whose succession independence was declared in 1991.
